newsitem.title: UK: Adams lauds Clinton on N.Ireland, no hint of truce.
newsitem.headline: Adams lauds Clinton on N.Ireland, no hint of truce.

text.p: Gerry Adams, head of the IRA's political arm, on Thursday welcomed U.S. President Clinton's plea for peace in Northern Ireland but gave no hint as to whether his outlawed Irish guerrilla allies would heed the call.
British and Irish ministers who had talks in Dublin firmly supported Clinton's appeal to the Irish Republican Army "to lay down their guns for good".
They were adamant that the IRA -- which scrapped a 17-month ceasefire in February last year -- must end its campaign of violence before Sinn Fein could win a seat in peace talks.
Clinton, speaking during a one-day visit to London at an open-air press conference with British Prime Minister Tony Blair, said the IRA could not "talk and shoot" at the same time.

Adams, who wants Britain to bring his Sinn Fein party into all-party peace talks immediately, issued a brief statement in Belfast which made no reference to the IRA but urged London to open the way to talks.
"I welcome President Clinton's continued and balanced support in the search for peace in Ireland. I agree with him that the search for peace should be done on a basis of inclusiveness," he said.
Irish foreign minister Dick Spring said he shared Clinton's hopes for all-party talks after an IRA ceasefire.

"We are going to need the co-operation of all the parties. We want Sinn Fein at the talks -- they know what has to be done to be at the table. And I would urge them to convince the IRA to declare a ceasefire as quickly as possible," he told reporters.

Spring was speaking after talks with Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam, who was visiting Dublin for the first time in her official role since her appointment four weeks ago following Blair's Labour Party's landslide election win.
The Northern Ireland multi-party peace talks reopen in Belfast next Tuesday after a three month adjournment. They are chaired by former U.S. senator George Mitchell.

Mowlam, in a statement issued in London, spoke of "the vital importance" of Clinton's co-operation in peace efforts and urged all Americans who wished Northern Ireland well to press Sinn Fein to seek an irrevocable end to IRA violence.

"Until Sinn Fein are able to do this and commit themselves exclusively to the path of peace and democracy they will not be in the talks in Northern Ireland -- and those talks will carry on without them," she said.

In Dublin, she declined to be drawn on earlier radio comments by Adams that Sinn Fein negotiators had made no headway in talks on Wedneday with senior officials from her Northern Ireland Office, held to try and revive battered peace hopes.

Britain, like Ireland, refuses to let its ministers meet Sinn Fein, although Blair has ended a 16-month ban on discussions involving officials to gauge whether Sinn Fein and the IRA were committed to taking the gun out of Irish politics.

Adams said Sinn Fein delegates did not get "the clarity they required" from the British officials on key demands for a date of entry to talks, and a guarantee that demands for a surrender of IRA arms would not be allowed to block full-scale talks.
The IRA is fighting to end Britain's rule of Northern Ireland, which the majority Protestant Unionists want to retain.
